adherence.reason: The text is a fictional narrative grounded in Revolutionary-era Paris and uses period figures, institutions, and public executions as its setting.
Thomas is explicitly a sixteen-year-old apprentice being trained by executioner Pierre in the mechanics and discipline of the trade.
The story repeatedly identifies the Revolution, revolutionary crowds, tricolor symbols, National Guardsmen, and executions of alleged traitors.
Pierre explicitly teaches Thomas never to look at condemned prisoners' faces before the blade falls and explains the rule's purpose.
All action unfolds continuously during one rainy, crowded public execution day as successive carts arrive.
The execution takes place before a large crowd in Paris's Place de la Concorde.
Thomas recognizes the next prisoner as Monsieur Henri, the baker who sheltered and fed him after his mother's death when he was an orphaned child.
The prohibited word does not appear in the story text; the apparatus is referred to as the machine, device, frame, or blade.
The final sentences say Thomas's previously steady hands begin to shake uncontrollably, explicitly contrasting this with the entire duration of his training.
